assumptions: The initial beachhead is limited to substantial Polish commercial renovation or demolition projects whose conservatively estimated recoverable value exceeds audit and coordination cost; small projects are screened out.

The company remains asset-light: it does not take title to or possession of salvage, and regulated waste work, hazardous-material work, engineering review, testing, removal, storage, and transport are performed by properly authorised and insured specialists or charged through to the customer.
The proposed 12000-25000 PLN audit fee, 3-8% completed-sale fee, 50-65% gross-margin range, buyer liquidity, and customer willingness to pay are unvalidated hypotheses rather than established facts.
No exclusive access to owners, contractors, buyers, inventory data, or regulatory rights is assumed, and Concular is treated as a close existing full-stack substitute.
The founder can commit 15-20 hours per week and approximately 75000 PLN for a partner-led pilot while retaining employment; meaningful scale would require an operating team.
Missing Polish demand, transaction, insurance, and field-productivity evidence is treated as uncertainty, not as proof that the model fails.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The insight that reuse options are won or lost during the owner-authorised interval before deinstallation, demolition, or waste classification is coherent, and charging for the audit avoids relying entirely on fragile marketplace commissions. However, EU guidance and Concular's existing integrated offer show that the workflow is recognised rather than a uniquely overlooked mechanism.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Polish sorting duties, fixed demolition dates, hazardous-material concerns, and the risk of mishandling product-versus-waste status create genuine owner and contractor coordination pain. The audit itself is not generally mandated, JRC found economic effectiveness uncertain, and no reviewed evidence establishes paid Polish demand, so willingness to pay for the proposed fee remains a central uncertainty.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: An upfront service fee, selective success fee, no inventory ownership, and pass-through specialist costs could support useful contribution margins and controlled setup capital. The 50-65% gross margin, ten-project cash payback, CAC, repeat rate, and 250-project wealth path are unvalidated; low reported marketplace order values, free or no-commission substitutes, and costly expert work make owner earnings and operating leverage uncertain.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Large Polish commercial sites with a fixed demolition date form a reasonably narrow, filterable beachhead, and portfolio owners or contractors can supply repeated projects. The evidence does not quantify the economically eligible project pool, recoverable-value distribution, or buyer density, so it is not yet clear that the subset capable of carrying a paid audit is large enough.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Local Polish legal triage, contractor relationships, and fast owner-authorised inventory could create a specialised regional position. Yet Concular already combines audits, AI-assisted inventory, marketplace distribution, logistics, and insured or warranted installation, while the candidate has no exclusive supply, buyer channel, or legal right that supports likely domination.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful beachhead could extend into additional component classes, reuse procurement, portfolio reporting, contractor software, adjacent Polish regions, and selected CEE markets using accumulated workflow data and partners. Expansion is moderated by route-specific construction-product, waste, testing, insurance, and logistics requirements that must be solved again across classes and jurisdictions.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Records of buyer acceptance criteria, removal yields, project timing, and lawful fallback routes could improve triage and quoting with volume, and embedded portfolio relationships could add switching friction. The core service is reproducible, the current data asset does not yet exist, incumbents can accumulate similar information, and a planned EU data platform may commoditise inventory data rather than reinforce exclusivity.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: A single accountable workflow for inventory, document recovery, legal routing, buyer reservation, and removal scheduling is more useful to a complex project than merely posting lots on an open marketplace. No evidence yet shows a decisive improvement in recovery value, cost, speed, risk, or schedule certainty, and the closest incumbent already offers a broader integrated stack.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Poland's 2025 construction-waste separation rules and broader EU movement toward selective demolition and digital pre-demolition audits create favourable attention and workflow pressure. Momentum is not the same as a purchase mandate, and future public audit infrastructure could also lower differentiation, so timing helps demand discovery more than it guarantees a durable business.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Winning a few demolition contractors, portfolio owners, architects, and licensed waste operators as design partners is a plausible concentrated route that fits the founder better than broad consumer acquisition and may expose forward project pipelines. There is no demonstrated channel access, CAC, repeatability, or local buyer liquidity, and every project still requires a deadline-sensitive two-sided match.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The inventory, computer-vision, evidence-reconciliation, and triage layers fit the founder's data skills, and a bounded pilot is plausible within the stated capital if field operations are delegated. Product liability, hazardous materials, BDO scope, engineering and insurance review, removal damage, logistics, and demolition scheduling require specialist accountability; exception-heavy coordination and eventual team building are a weak fit for long-term part-time operation.

main_structural_strength: The model controls the short owner-authorised window before demolition and monetises a paid decision-and-coordination service, allowing it to reject uneconomic sites and avoid owning inventory rather than depending on a thin general marketplace take rate.
primary_score_limiter: There is no evidence yet that enough Polish owners will pay an audit fee on sites with sufficient recoverable value to cover specialist-heavy delivery, buyer acquisition, and deadline risk, so attractive repeat economics remain unestablished.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: JRC reports audit costs of roughly EUR 3000-5000 for demolition projects up to EUR 300000 while finding effectiveness and economic benefit uncertain and warning of disproportionate burden for small projects; because the audit is not generally mandated, this directly challenges the payer case.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Signed and paid engagements from at least three independent Polish owners or demolition contractors across a representative pipeline of roughly twenty sites, with site-level evidence on recoverable value, field and specialist cost, inventory time, buyer-match and completed-sale rates, cancellations, contribution margin, CAC/payback, and repeat pipeline, plus written Polish legal and insurer guidance defining eligible component classes and the product-versus-waste and BDO contract flow.
highest_value_structural_change: Convert the one-off audit brokerage into a portfolio-level staged service: charge a recurring pipeline-screening retainer, advance to a full paid audit only when a conservative value-to-delivery-cost hurdle is met, limit the first wedge to pre-sellable non-structural component classes, and place any waste handling under one licensed operator of record.
